title: Bioenergetics and Regulation of Metabolism
scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT biochemistry lessons covering the declared outline sections. This release is implemented, not independently scientifically verified; it is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: For a defined reaction, actual free energy depends on composition: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q under a consistent biochemical standard-state convention.
A negative actual ΔG favors the written forward direction under the stated conditions. A negative standard value alone does not determine direction at every concentration.
At equilibrium, actual ΔG is zero and the reaction quotient equals the equilibrium constant. Zero net flux does not require molecular motion or exchange to stop.
Coupled reaction free energies add when stoichiometries are combined correctly. Thermodynamic favorability does not specify how quickly the process occurs.

steps.text: ATP hydrolysis can be coupled to otherwise unfavorable processes through a shared intermediate or molecular mechanism. Merely putting two unrelated reactions together does not guarantee coupling.
Favorable hydrolysis reflects the free-energy balance between reactants and products, including resonance, solvation and charge effects. Breaking a bond itself requires energy.
ATP to ADP and phosphate differs from ATP to AMP and pyrophosphate. Subsequent pyrophosphate hydrolysis can help drive biosynthetic activation steps.
ATP is regenerated continuously and is an energy-transfer currency. It is not the principal long-term mass storage form of fuel in the body.

steps.text: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain. An oxidizing agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced; a reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidized.

steps.text: After a mixed meal, insulin tends to favor nutrient uptake and storage. During fasting, hormonal and substrate changes favor mobilization and maintenance of blood glucose.
Early fasting draws on hepatic glycogen and gluconeogenesis. As glycogen becomes depleted, gluconeogenesis and increasing ketone availability become more important.
Tissues adapt differently: muscle can use fatty acids, while red blood cells continue to require glycolysis. The brain can use more ketones during prolonged fasting but still has glucose needs.
Time boundaries vary with prior diet, activity and physiology. These state labels describe trends, not exact universal hourly cutoffs.

steps.text: Liver buffers circulating fuel supply through storage, glucose production and ketone production, depending on state. It is not simply a duplicate of skeletal muscle metabolism.
Skeletal muscle uses its own glycogen and can oxidize fatty acids. Its net fuel choice changes with exercise intensity, substrate availability and hormonal state.
The brain normally relies heavily on glucose and can use ketones during prolonged fasting. Long-chain fatty acids are not its major routine oxidative fuel.
Mature human red blood cells lack mitochondria, so they obtain ATP through glycolysis and produce lactate. They cannot perform mitochondrial beta oxidation or oxidative phosphorylation.

steps.text: In the Cori cycle, lactate produced by tissues such as exercising muscle or red blood cells reaches liver and can supply gluconeogenesis. Glucose can then return to peripheral tissues.
Liver glucose synthesis from lactate consumes energy, whereas peripheral glycolysis yields ATP. The cycle redistributes fuel and metabolic work rather than generating free energy for the body.
The glucose–alanine cycle transfers both carbon and nitrogen from muscle toward liver. Nitrogen disposal and carbon recycling must be accounted for separately.
Integrated metabolism requires tissue, compartment, hormone and substrate context. For a perturbation, follow carbon, electrons and ATP costs separately before predicting whole-body effects.
